utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam, and good afternoon to you. Mr. Oric, usual question, are you receiving interpretation in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen, I can hear the interpretation in my own language and I understand it completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, and you may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, I'm Patricia Sellers for the Prosecution. With me today is Ms. Joanne Richardson who is co-counsel and Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink who is our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam, and good afternoon for you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Appearing on behalf of Naser Oric are Mrs. Vasvija Vidovic, lead counsel, Mr. John Jones, co-counsel, and with us are Adisa Mehic our legal assistant and Mr. Geoff Roberts, CaseMap manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam, and good afternoon to you and your team. So any preliminaries before we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we do have some preliminaries and they are basically announcements. I would like to tell you that we have informed the Defence counsel of these announcements. First of all, we will be handing up hard copies of the transcripts of the Oric interview, which means P328 and P329. In addition to that we would like to bring your attention that P329 included a videotape, number 7, which was actually duplicated, meaning that we had two videotapes number 7 but it was put under the heading of videotape number 8 and today we are rectifying that. In that manner the interview that took place on the morning of May 21st 2001 is now correctly entitled videotape number 8 and this is part of ERN number V002920. This should substitute -- this number 8 tape we are handing up today should substitute for the number 8 tape that was handed up on the 10th of January and that has also been explained to the Registrar. The last thing I would like to inform the Trial Chamber of is that there were a series of translations that numbered 38 and they were translations that had not accompanied the Prosecution exhibits. They were English translations and they also are being handed up today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Ms. Sellers. Any remarks from your side? Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. No comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Omerovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will be -- and others will be also speaking in English and while we speak what we are saying is being interpreted to you or should be interpreted to you in your language. I want to make sure first and foremost that you are receiving interpretation in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am receiving interpretation in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. If at any time during these proceedings while you are here there are problems with your receiving interpretation, please draw our attention straight away and we will rectify it. I welcome you to this Tribunal and also to this Trial Chamber which is presiding over the trial against Naser Oric. You are a witness for the Prosecution, you have been summoned by the Prosecution, and as a witness of this Tribunal, you are required before you start giving evidence to make a solemn declaration equivalent to an oath, in the sense that in the course of your testimony, you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. As an ex-judge, I don't need to explain this to you. You are going to be handed the text of the declaration. Please read it out in a way that we can hear you and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please take a seat. Ms. Richardson is going first and she will ask you a series of questions. I understand she is going to finish with her questions today. She will then be followed by Madam Vidovic tomorrow who will be cross-examining you, and she's lead counsel for Naser Oric. Ms. Richardson, you can lead the witness in the initial part as regards the straightforward questions which I take it will not be contested.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Omerovic, please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Mensud Omerovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Please could be confirm the following information with either yes or no. You were born on the 3rd of January, 1965.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1963, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: 1963, excuse me. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's correct, 1963?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You were married and you are of Muslim ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You have two children?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You are a lawyer and also a former judge?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You are presently a lawyer, correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You were born in Kruseva Do but you later moved with your family to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And you resided in Bratunac until 1992?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You presently reside in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: With respect to your criminal -- excuse me, your military training, you completed this in October of 1981 and that was with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm now going to go over your professional experience. You were a student and graduated from the faculty of law in Sarajevo in 1987?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: You worked as an intern in the offence court of Bratunac ... [microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I seem to have lost the audio.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can hear you now. Thank you. I could hear you before but not through the headphones.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic could you please confirm that you worked as an intern in the office of the offence court in Bratunac in 1987 and then you continued working there for two and a half years? You need to answer verbally so it can be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what type of offences -- if you could just briefly tell Your Honours that you were involved with in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: The misdemeanour court has the jurisdiction over offences prescribed by law. First and foremost, traffic violations, as defined by the law on traffic safety. Then issues dealing with public order, prescribed by that piece of legislation. And misdemeanour contained in the tax law as well as the offences in the law on the use of natural resources such as water, forests, et cetera. And the sanctions are prescribed for the violations of these provisions. That is the real jurisdiction of the misdemeanour court and there is also the basic act regulating the procedure before such a court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: For the two and a half years, could you tell us what your duties were in that court? What was your main function, without going into too much detail?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't receive the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's the only way of doing it. Either you or I can read it out and the interpreters will translate it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question was the following: For the two and a half years could you tell us what your duties were in that court? What was your main function, without going into much detail?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First I worked as an intern with the misdemeanour court for a year, after which I took the exam to become a judge in a misdemeanour court and then I continued for another year and a half to work as an expert associate. So I presided over misdemeanour proceedings and I would issue decisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Following that position in the Court of the offence court of Bratunac also referred to as the misdemeanour court, could you confirm that you were a lawyer for the office for commerce and social affairs in 1990 and following that position you worked as an inspector for taxation in Bratunac in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For six months I worked with the department for commerce and social affairs, with the municipality of Bratunac, and then since 1991 until the war broke out I worked as an inspector with the tax authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, following your position in Bratunac in 1991, as an inspector, could you also confirm the following information, and I'm keeping this somewhat brief. I understand that there may have been other incidents that occurred during this period of time but we are short on time. If you could confirm that you left Bratunac because -- in April of 1992 because there were tensions in the area, in your village and the surrounding villages as well?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: I left Bratunac on the 11th of April and the reason for leaving Bratunac was that I was afraid for my own security because the local Serbs set up checkpoints on all exits from the town, that is on all the streets that one could take to get out of the town. There they established checkpoints with armed personnel and immediately prior to the 11th of April, Zvornik was attacked. A few days earlier and perhaps 20 days earlier, the same happened in Bijeljina and I thought Bratunac was next because it was the next town by the Drina. So I was afraid that the Serb forces would attack Bratunac and that I wouldn't be able to get out. And out of fear for my own life and the safety of my family I decided to leave Bratunac and to stay with our family in the country near Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And you arrived in Srebrenica in mid-July 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Having spent three months in the village of Krusev Dol with my uncle and since there was the general shortage of food - his family didn't have enough for themselves - so I decided to move to Srebrenica together with my wife and son, since the Serb forces withdrew from Srebrenica and it seemed there was -- there were abandoned apartments that we could be accommodated in. So by mid-June we were in Srebrenica and we came from that village in which I spent the three months.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Prior to your arrival in Srebrenica in July of 1992, had you been to Srebrenica before?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: I did quite often. Srebrenica is ten kilometres away from Bratunac so I went there frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Srebrenica, you testified that you were in an apartment. Could you tell us if you know who the owner of that apartment was?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if my colleague from the Prosecution would not pose questions leading the witness from now on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe I asked who the owner of the apartment was. I don't believe that's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't see any validity in your objection.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's proceed. Let's proceed with your question and with the answer. I don't think we can sustain the objection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After having come to Srebrenica, I spent the night in an apartment in which my sister and my brother-in-law were accommodated as refugees. They were in a Muslim apartment. It was a very small apartment, studio-type apartment. We spent the night there and then the sister of a woman who lived in the same building found out that there was an empty apartment available from which a Serb family left earlier. They took their things with them and left for Serbia. The key to the apartment was in possession of that other woman in the building and until our arrival, there was a woman in the apartment from one of the villages around Srebrenica because her village was in danger so she fled. But since the village was not burned down, she returned. So the apartment stayed empty. We got the key and we moved in. It was a larger apartment with two completely empty rooms. There were only two very old couches, and a wooden stove and a bit of other furniture. That's all that was in the apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were there many other such apartments that had been abandoned?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of April, based on my knowledge, Srebrenica was left by almost all Bosniaks and Serbs because the Serbs took over. So even a greater portion of the Serb population left prior to the combat activities. So most of the apartments were empty.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And who occupied these apartments? You said you and your family occupied one of them. Who occupied the other apartments? And if you could tell us what month you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: I came in July. Perhaps on the 15th or the 17th I arrived to Srebrenica, and there were a lot of refugees in Srebrenica at the time from the municipality of Bratunac from the villages of Voljevica, Zaluzje, Bilice, Prisulja [phoen], Tegare and so on and so forth. I saw those people because I knew a lot of them from before. They fled at the very beginning to the villages surrounding Srebrenica such as Mocevice, Podloznik, Strozersko, et cetera. They were accommodated in the houses of the people who lived in those villages so these houses were very full. There were up to 20 or 30 refugees per house, and since they had no room to sleep, they had to sleep on the floor. They ran out of food very quickly, the food that those people who lived in those houses prior to that had. And as soon as the Serbs left Srebrenica, I don't know exactly what month that was in 1992, but those people simply moved from those houses where they why accommodated temporarily to the town so that they could find accommodation because in those villages they did not even have the bare necessities and I was told this personally by my sister who did live in such a house in the village of Mocevice where there were over 20 people and they had to sleep on the floor and they had no food left.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: For all of 1992, and when I say all I should say from the time you arrived in Srebrenica, July, August, through December, were most of the refugees living in these apartments that had been abandoned?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In apartments and in houses. There were also very many empty houses. My wife's sister lived in an empty house which belonged to her family in Srebrenica, there were also very many Muslim flats and houses and people had friends who gave them their house keys and then they moved in. My brother and his family moved into a Bosniak flat belonging to a colleague of his who had left for Tuzla in April. This friend of his had an apartment and he allowed my brother to move into it with his family. My sister also lived in a Bosniak flat in the same building I was living in. My wife's sister was in a Bosniak house belonging to relatives of hers. So people who had relatives or friends would get house keys from them and then they would go and live in those flats and houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just staying on the housing issue with respect to refugees for one moment, could you tell us if they came a point in time, just very briefly, when the refugees -- where there was no more apartments or houses available and the refugees were -- were some place else?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: In September, perhaps, there was a wave of refugees from the Zepa and Han Pijesak area. There were fierce attacks on those villages. Parts of those villages were burned down. People were expelled and they set out Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. towards Srebrenica which was some sort of free territory and then sometime around September, very many refugees arrived to the town centre from those areas and people simply went to live wherever they could. This was bearable until the time in 1993 when there was a fierce offensive against Srpska, Konjevic Polje, Glogova, in the Bratunac municipality and other villages in the Bratunac municipality, Podloznik, parts of Pirici and the villages overlooking Srebrenica. This was a large, free area, and all these people fled the Serb attacks. They left their houses, their houses were burned, they all arrived in Srebrenica, and the situation was disastrous. There was no accommodation left anywhere. People remained outdoors. It was snowing. They lit fires, they used books, paper, whatever they could find, to feed the fires and women and children sat around these fires and it was a very, very upsetting sight to see all this. They would sit there all night.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you arrived in Srebrenica in July of 1992, were you aware of the presence of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Some kind of organisation did exist. It was in fact a village organisation. As the Serbs attacked and set fire to parts of villages, the people who fled gathered together in the villages that remained free and they simply agreed with each other that they had to resist, that they had to defend themselves or they would be killed. So all of these villages or groups of villages had their own local unit of sorts to defend the village. That was what was like in Kruseva Do where I spent the first three months. People simply gathered in a field and when they realised we would all be killed, we gathered together and one of those men was elected kind of commander and then some sort of guards or night patrols were organised at the approaches to the village. But there was all very poorly organised. There weren't any weapons. People had some hunting weapons, perhaps, but they didn't want to lend them to other people. People would fail to turn up for guard duty and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I need to stop you here because I need you to respond to my question with respect to Srebrenica only. We are running short of time, so if you could limit your answer to your knowledge of the Territorial Defence in Srebrenica, I'd greatly appreciate it. Now, did you learn whether or not the Srebrenica had a Territorial Defence and whether anyone -- whether there was a commander of that Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't observe on my arrival in Srebrenica that there was some sort of command. I really didn't notice any such thing. In the village, there were some kind of village units around Srebrenica but in Srebrenica itself, I really was not aware of the existence of any kind of command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you learn of anyone by the name of Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What did you learn his role was, if any, in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: I learned that the local people, the local village commanders, or whatever you might call them, the leaders of the village defence, had a meeting and agreed that Naser should be the main commander for the entire defence. Somebody who would be the main man. I learned that from citizens.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know Naser Oric before this period of time, in July of 1992, before your arrival in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, I would see him around. I didn't know him personally. I would see him around town. He was driving a Renault 5. He used to drive fast. I didn't know him personally. I didn't have a chance to meet him personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time that you were -- while you were in Srebrenica that you were approached about the establishment of a court for Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: At one point in time, I think I was on my way to get water. As we were short of water, we had to go to a fountain and queue up to get water, and as I was on my way there, I met Professor Nijaz Masic. He was a professor of history - I knew him from before the war - and he told me that he wanted a court to be established in Srebrenica. He actually said a military court martial. I told him I didn't know there were any such things as military court martials. Probably somebody who was not a lawyer and who was ignorant of the law used that expression. I said there were military courts, military prosecutors' offices and if somebody wanted to establish a court it had to be a regular military court and there also had to be an appeals court, that there had to be a military Prosecutor and so on and so forth, that this had to follow a regular, legal procedure in compliance with the legislation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Probably somebody who was ignorant, because I know that in the last war, the Partisans had in their units court martials which punished a soldier if he stole something or did something else, and the commander would pass judgement on the spot. So probably somebody in their ignorance used that expression, military court martial, but in the legal framework, there is no such thing provided for.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, I'd like to just go back just briefly to a series of questions. You mentioned - we will get back to the court in a moment - you mentioned that there was a shortage of food in Srebrenica during the time you were present and I'd like you to keep your answer as brief as possible. Could you tell the Trial Chamber how the -- how it was that people went about getting food in Srebrenica? And if you could be as brief as possible, I'd appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in Srebrenica in July, there was absolutely no food there. The Srebrenica area is not very well supplied with food. The area around Srebrenica is farm country and up until October, people would go to the village of Voljevica under cover of night. In the Bratunac municipality, they would pass through the Chetnik lines through the woods. Columns of some ten people would go to the village of Voljevica from which the inhabitants had been expelled and they would collect corn, wheat, whatever they found in sacks and by night they would bring this to Srebrenica. Once when I was short of food, I myself went to the village of Voljevica by night with one such group. It was really a very unpleasant experience. We walked through the beds of streams, through the woods, it was night, and when we approached the village, there were Chetniks down there. They noticed us and opened fire. Then they set fire to a house. We got scared and started to flee and then I lost my glasses and the glass broke. We managed to collect some maize and some wheat in front of a house. The maize was used as cattle feed and at around midnight, we set out to return to Srebrenica along the same route. It started to rain. It was dark. You couldn't see anything. And at one point the Chetniks saw us and we fled every which way. I threw away what I was carrying and I arrived in Srebrenica without anything. Some people managed to bring back something and I never dared go down that way again because it was truly a terrifying experience. However, until October, as long as there was food there, people would take that route by night, including women and old children, and that's how they would get food. There was a little food that you could get from the local population who had remained in their homes, but these were purely symbolic quantities because they themselves were short of food. On several occasions I would visit acquaintances or my wife's relatives and they would give us a kilogram or two of flour and perhaps a few vegetables and it was barely enough to survive on. So we were constantly hungry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'd like to bring your attention specifically to December of 1992, the area of Loznica Rijeka. Do you recall that period -- period of time in that area?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that. I have to say something before I go into that. In October I went to get water in the morning, and I saw that the town was empty. I found this strange. There was no one around, only an elderly woman or two or an old man, and then I found out that on that day, there was an operation to get food in the villages of Zanjevo, Abdulici, Fakovici, and all the people had left the town. I didn't even know that people were going there in search of food, and secondly, this was far away. I was not physically fit enough and I wasn't used to finding my way about. However, in December, when there was an action, when there was no food left in the town, and an action was organised to get food, I set out by night from Srebrenica. It was about 4 a.m., and I went through the old town. We arrived at the village of Pribicevac and then we went downhill next to the village, and when dawn broke - it was about 7.00 in the morning - we were in front of the village of Podloznik. All of a sudden, in our immediate vicinity, some 20 or 30 metres away, three shells landed. Huge shells. And they wounded a woman who was right next to me. Her name is Hajra. We carried her into a house. There was a garage downstairs. The house was unfinished, and some 20 of us took shelter there. We bandaged her leg. She had been wounded in the leg by shrapnel, and as shells were falling, you could hear planes dropping bombs. We didn't dare go any further. We went to a Bosniak house which was nearby in the village of Podloznik and I spent a few hours there, and then simply I didn't dare go any further. So in the afternoon, I went back towards Srebrenica. At about a kilometre away from Podloznik, when I was on my way back, a small plane with two wings appeared above us and started shooting at us. It was a biplane, and there was a column of men, women and children, including elderly men, the plane was flying low over head, a hundred or two hundred metres up, and they fired at us from machine-guns. I tried to hide in a haystack but I couldn't get into it. It was terrible, it was really terrible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Omerovic. Let me stop you so I could pose another question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could the witness possibly remember the exact date of this event?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If you could please, Mr. Omerovic, answer His Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's told us he's referring to events in December. I'm not sure, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: December. Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, do you recall the day -- the exact day in December that this occurred?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: This was sometime in mid-December, maybe the 14th or the 15th. In the middle of December. It could have been the 14th, it might have been the 15th. I can't be 100 per cent certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Judge Eser?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name of this village because it did not appear on our transcript. The name of the village where you went to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Podloznik. I didn't get as far as the Loznica river or Bjelovac, I simply arrived in the village of Podloznik. It was a Bosniak village which was still inhabited at the time. The people still hadn't been expelled. I didn't go as far as the Loznica river because there was already shelling there and the bombing, so I didn't dare go there, neither I nor the people who were with me in that group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Who conducted the operations you just testified about? You state that operations were conducted you noticed in October that the town was empty as well. Could you tell Your Honours who conducted the operations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he knows.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If you know.

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know who. I can't say who conducted the operations. I really couldn't confirm that, because what I know about this, well, I was not involved in that in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: How did people learn of the operations?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: In Srebrenica, it was difficult to tell soldiers and civilians apart because people lived with their families. Some people went to stand guard. Others didn't. There was never an army that was established with responsibility, with order, an army like the one I served in before. People continued to live in their houses. If they had a weapon they kept it at home. They went on living with their families and you could never be certain whether someone was in the army or not. There were large numbers of people living in my building who never went to participate in any kind of operation, and some people did. It was only those who were duty-bound, who had lived in the villages surrounding Srebrenica which were directly on the front line, it was those people who went to take up shifts. But in the town itself, there was never any kind of military organisation, and there was no one who could mobilise those people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, let's just clarify. The witness is using the word "action" all the time and the Prosecutor is persistently using the word "operation." Could we have this clarified?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the witness said "operation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Do you distinguish between an operation and an action, Mr. Omerovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Terminologically, those are two different things. An operation in my view implies an expert team. It implies professionally developed plans, some kind of hierarchy, organisation, and so on and so forth. These were actions to get food, to survive in a city that was under siege, because no food and no aid arrived from anywhere. Until October, food was brought from the village of Voljevica, a Muslim village in Bratunac municipality. I know that for three days food was taken from the villages of Zanjevo and Abdulici, because that was a very wealthy village, and for three days people went to the villages of Jago [phoen] and Osalo [phoen] because three days after this action I went to see my wife's family in the village of Jagonja [phoen] and they gave me a little food because they had brought it up from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Well, you've got an answer from him as to regards -- as regards operations and actions. And he seems to be talking of actions but he did mention operation before so if you want to direct the question to him, what he meant by that, you're free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it is necessary, because I think the matter has been superseded. Yes, Madam Vidovic

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness used the word "action". It was interpreted as "operations." That's why I intervened, among other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So if it's a question of interpretation, I suppose we can move forward.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, were soldiers involved in the actions?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: The people who lived in Srebrenica, who had weapons, for example, to be specific, when this action to get food was carried out, I was in a column together with women, men, elderly men, even children, ten year old children. I also saw men with weapons. Perhaps we could call them soldiers. These soldiers in Srebrenica had wives, children, parents, families in Srebrenica, and they were trying to get hold of food. These actions in essence had as their main goal to get food, enough food to survive until the issue of Srebrenica was solved. We were expecting someone to solve the issue of Srebrenica because we were unable to defend ourselves and we had nothing to live on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to bring you back at this time to the discussion about the Court that you had with Professor Masic, if I'm pronouncing his name correctly, and if I am not, please correct me. After you told him that there was no such thing as a military court martial, what was his response?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: He told me that he would pass this on to someone. Professor Masic had fled from Bratunac, from the village of Voljevica where he had lived until the war, and he was -- he had been in Srebrenica throughout this time and he knew the people who were working in the municipalities, people who were important in some way. When I arrived in mid-July, I didn't know anyone so he told me he would pass this on to someone. I don't know who, but that's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did there come a time that you were asked again about this -- about establishing a court? And could you tell us the Trial Chamber when that was?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: At the session of the War Presidency, I was invited by a colleague of mine, a good friend who had been at university with me, and at that time he was the secretary of the War Presidency. His name was Esad Nukic. I can't remember the exact date but there are minutes from that session and he told me that there would be some discussion about the establishing of a court and that it might be a good idea if I were to attend and provide an explanation. I attended this one session where one of the items on the agenda was the issue of the so-called military court martial.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Okay. Before we get to this agenda, could you tell Your Honours who was present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Present at the meeting were several people. It included too many people. My impression was that this was a meeting in which there were other participants, not only members of the War Presidency but also the representatives of the villages who organised their defence, and from each Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the villages there was a -- one representative. That's the impression I got. There was also Avdic Hajrudin who was the president of the War Presidency. Then there was the secretary as well as Osman Osmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Let me just stop you. If you know, could you tell Your Honours what the position held by each person you naming as present at the meeting. For instance, Osman Osmanovic, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hasn't that been established by other witnesses? Do we need to re-establish it again by means of this witness? I don't know. It's up to you. You're free to make your question but if this has already been --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I understand your point but I do think it's important to -- as a follow-up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you know what position Osman Osmanovic held?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Until that moment, I didn't know that, but then and there I learned that he held the function of the head of the TO staff of Srebrenica. That's when I found out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Fine. And who else was at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Hamed Salihovic was present. Then Nijaz Masic. There was a representative from the postal office, Hamed Alic, and I can't remember the rest. Yes, there was Zulfo Tursunovic and some other people, representatives from the villages. I believe there was also Mirsad Dudic and perhaps Nedzad Bektic but I'm not sure. So there were several people comprising 15 or even 20 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you recall the date of this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: I can't recall precisely. It may have been in November, maybe even early December. So the end of November, the beginning of December. I can't be more precise since a lot of time had elapsed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like the usher's assistance, I will be -- we will be using with this witness P84. And we would ask that the English be placed on the ELMO. English version, I would ask the ushers to place the document starting on page 19 and it's dated 19th of November, 1992. For the purposes of the witness, it's ERN 02115068. I would like the witness to look at -- just for the record I will put the ERN number with respect to the English. I believe it's 02115068 as well, page 19. We do have another ERN number. If I could have a moment, Your Honour. All right. That's the ERN number we will be using.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, if you could look at pages -- I will be directing you to pages in the B/C/S version, ERN number 02115068, 69, 70, 71 and 72. Prior to -- my first question is, prior to your arrival in The Hague, had you seen this document, specifically this excerpt, before?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If you could just -- well, let's take it one page at a time. Beginning on the first page, it's dated -- and that's page 19 of the English, the date is 9th of November 1992. It states "meeting of the joint" -- "meeting of the War Presidency and the Srebrenica armed forces staff." There is an agenda. If you could look at the agenda, 1 through 8, and tell Your Honours if this represents the discussion or the items that were discussed in that meeting you just testified about?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Go to the next page. 039 -- excuse me, 03090724. This is page 20 of the English version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: So we can follow, Your Honour, is this witness saying that he was at this meeting? We had the -- whether it's the discussion or the list of the issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is how I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps he could be asked directly so we could follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. Mr. Omerovic, just to clarify this, you have been directed specifically to what appear to be minutes of a meeting or joint meeting of the War Presidency and the Srebrenica Armed Forces Staff that allegedly took place on the 9th of November 1992. It's being put to you that you answered the previous question that this is the correct agenda because you were present at that meeting. Do you recall being present at this particular meeting of the 9th of November 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That was the meeting. The first meeting that I attended, I was invited to offer some clarification on the forming of the Court. That is the agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact, you already mentioned his surname is mentioned later on at the end of -- anyway, go ahead, Ms. Richardson, please. And we need to have a break in 2 or 3 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'll keep that in mind. I'll just ask one question before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. No, it's Sorry it's quarter to 4,00, not 3.30.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So 15 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 15, 17 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Do you see the name Hamed Salihovic on this document? I -- I do believe it is on page, the first page of the B/C/S, towards the end. Possibly -- actually, I'm mistaken. It's in the middle of the first page of the B/C/S. Mr. Omerovic, do you see the name Hamed Salihovic, right after the list of the agenda?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at the beginning, right after the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it states in the document you're reviewing that Hamed Salihovic submitted a report on the visit by some members of the command of the Srebrenica armed forces to Konjevic Polje and Cerska. It also -- it also states that Avdic, if you see the president's name there, I'm reading about four lines down, stated he supported the formation of the subregion and the units of the armed forces but he's against appointing people in this way. Now, just briefly, could you tell us, as you look at this discussion, by the different individuals mentioned, does this reflect what was discussed about -- was there discussion, I should say, about the creation of the subregion and about the subregion itself?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Hamed Salihovic submitted an extensive report on the visit of a delegation of sorts. I didn't understand at the time what that delegation was. I wasn't familiar with the situation. But apparently they visited Konjevic Polje and Cerska. The problem was that those areas were also surrounded and in a similar situation. As far as I understood, they spoke with some people there because they were cut off from Tuzla and the rest of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were discussing how to jointly work in order to organise defence, and at the same time, Hamed Salihovic spoke about a political hierarchy or formation of a subregion which was contrary to the laws that were in force on the way local self-governance should be organised. They were talking about either a subregion being formed or that it should be formed, and so he submitted an extensive report.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, my next question is, if you would take a look at on the B/C/S version it's ERN number 02115069, on that page, there is a reference or a statement by Hamed Salihovic. It states, "I swear I do not know the reasons for leaving. The formation of the subregion is legal and logical continuation of the activities carried out so far. The names are not important and voting took place." Now, do you see the list of the three names that are mentioned here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what was read by the Prosecutor is an interpretation of what the -- it doesn't exist in the Bosnian original. Perhaps I can read it into the microphone. Maybe the Prosecutor couldn't read what was -- perhaps the translation was incorrect but this is not the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... what we need, because -- I appreciate you raising this matter, but in order to be able to follow properly, I think the interpreters themselves ought to have visible the text in its original handwritten format. So we either have it on Sanction or we have it on the ELMO. And what I suggest, Madam Vidovic, is that you read out -- don't try to translate. Read out the Serbo-Croat text as you read it and the interpreters will try to translate for us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, play I make another suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Not to be contrary, but perhaps the witness can read it, if he can, so we don't get any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've had the problem before, practically all the witnesses we have had here have not been able to read it. So, but of course if he can read it, then he can -- if he doesn't agree with Madam Vidovic's reading, he can point out any discrepancies himself and then we'll get the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But let's follow -- all right. Yeah. Yes, Madam Vidovic, if you can kindly start reading the part from 02115069 where Hamed Salihovic says whatever he says.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I could kindly ask that the witness follow. The Bosnian text says, "Hamed S. I swear I didn't know the reasons for going there. The forming of the subregion is the legal and logical continuation of the activities so far. Names are unimportant."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And how does this differ from what we have --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- in the -- the substance is exactly the same, I see. I mean, I don't know if Mr. Jones perhaps -- I don't know what has been going on between you but --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I could point out at least two words that are different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are talking of substance, not of --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at least the way it was interpreted into Bosnian, the words of the Prosecution were "I swear I didn't know about the reasons of the forming of the subregion," and it's completely different. It says here "I didn't know the reasons for going there." Full stop. "The forming of the subregion is a legal continuation of the activities so far."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... it's the same. I mean, the problem was not you reading out something which did not exist. The problem seems to have been the interpreters did not catch up with you in time and they amalgamated the first and second sentences together.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the meaning, the significance, was -- became different anyway.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's clear now, I think it's clear. You were referring the witness to those three names that appear on the diary or call it, whatever, the minutes, and the three names are Naser O, Hamed S, Zulfo S.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And we are reading from, of course, the English version. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If you could read, Mr. Omerovic, from the B/C/S version and tell -- tell Your Honours if you recall these individuals being present, who they are, first of all - if you know - and whether voting did take place that you recall.

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Looking at the minutes, the way they are presented here and then the way they were kept, it is unclear to me why these people are mentioned here. What voting, for what, how. It just says "voting took place," and then we have first names and just an initials and Naser O is probably Naser Oric. Hamed S is probably Hamed Salihovic and Zulfo S is Zulfo Salihovic. But I cannot recall as to whether the vote took place and how it was voted, and why they were elected.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He didn't answer the other part of the question. Assuming for the time being that these three names were the three persons that you mentioned, that is Naser Oric, Hamed Salihovic and Zulfo Salihovic, were these -- do you recall these three persons being present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The minutes in this particular meeting? You have that meeting in mind, of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I have this particular meeting of the 9th of November at which you were present. Here we say -- we have "voting took place" and then we have three names. Naser O, Hamed S, Zulfo S. You have told us who in your opinion these three persons are. You ever also said that you cannot recall whether they were elected, whether there was any voting, that -- you can't recall anything insofar as their possible election is concerned. But do you recall these three persons being present at that meeting, because they could have been elected without being present.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Naser Oric was definitely not present at the meeting, whereas Hamed Salihovic was. He submitted that extensive report of the activities. And as for the third person, I really cannot recall because there were several people there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Omerovic, I would like to turn your attention to another part of the -- this document, and I believe this is -- the portion I'm going to refer you to is located on 02115070. On the English version, it's 0211570, of course, and on page 21 -- actually, if you could look at the page just before that, if you look at the bottom of page 02115069, continuation is on the page 0211570. There is a reference, and I'm going to read six lines from the bottom of that particular section that I'm referring to. It states, and this is being said by Zulfo Tursunovic, I believe, who you said was present. "Some individuals are taking the law into their own hands." Do you see that sentence? If you could answer verbally so we are all on the same -- looking at the same material.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just say the witness did also refer to Zulfo Salihovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One is with an S. The other is with a Z.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I myself was confused initially until he said "Salihovic," but we have encountered both names in the past already but I think I --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think in the B/C/S, even, Salihovic is with a Z.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd prefer my learned friend not to guess at who -- which Zulfo it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's the case I did not intervene because obviously, to me, one is with an S, the other one is with a Z. But if, as you're saying they are both with a Z, or Z as they say in the States, then obviously you cannot assume who is who, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Point taken, Your Honour, and the witness can tell us who said that particular -- who said that. He was there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I admire your optimism, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, just while I'm on my feet. Also, it shouldn't be taken as read either that anyone said what's reported here. If the witness could be asked if he recalls. Naturally, because my learned friend just said this was said and we don't know if this was said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: According to the minutes, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, according to the minutes and what I'm -- and the document that I'm reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: If you could take a look at that particular section that starts with Zulfo, "Some individuals are taking the law into their own hands, this will continue to happen as long as the police are not doing their job." Unfortunately in the English version there is a word crossed out so I can only begin from the next sentence, "he mentioned several instances of breach of law and order, I have 11 outlaws who have stolen," and then there is a reference to oil, "broken into a school, now they are stealing sheep. The military court must start operating." And next, there is the name Osman appears and there is a -- some language, may or may not have been said by him but in the document it's next to his name. It states, "There are cases of abuse of power. Some individuals are not -- respects decisions and our self will, the court must start operating. This will -- this is still a long way to go to rule of law so we have to do the best we can. " [as read] And I will stop there. Do you recall that discussion taking place at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: There was discussion on this topic as well at the meeting, concerning the problems of structuring the police that stopped operating at the beginning of April, as well as all of the other bodies of authority, the police, the judiciary, the executive authorities. They all stopped with work. There was the state of chaos, nothing was functioning. So they discussed this because the head of police, Becir Bogilovic was also present at the meeting. And this was probably said by Zulfo Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Tursunovic. He expressed those problems. He mentioned that there should be a way found in order to establish such bodies, to deal with these problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whenever it's convenient for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: This is fine, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a 25-minute break. Everyone please try to be punctual so that we try to recover a little bit of the lost time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's continue and Ms. Richardson please try to avoid proving again what has been proved abundantly by many other witnesses already and stick to the real purpose for which you brought this witness here, which according to the declaration that we have here is on the court system.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And do I believe that this area of examination is important with respect to what occurred in the meeting of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we lost the first hour on what was happening in the area roughly starting from round about April et cetera. I mean, when --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll try my best to move as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to finish today. So it's -- there is no question about it. I will -- come 7.00, that will be the end.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if my co-counsel Ms. Sellers would like to give the Court some information about scheduling that may impact on Your Honour's decision at this point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to address you at the end of this session but for your information we will be calling one of our Office of the Prosecutor investigators, as you know on the schedule, and we anticipate that that will not take a court day. That will probably take, at least for the Prosecution side, a half hour at most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which one is this?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Mr. Gamini Wijeyesinghe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you had indicated one hour next week.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, that will take probably less time. And it -- I'm -- can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's next week.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, Your Honour. But also there is another witness we will be addressing you about tomorrow morning and there is a possibility with a very slight change also in schedule that we'll have a bit more ability to have court time in case there is any indication of running over and we will end on schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sellers, I hate being difficult, but you had indicated three hours for this witness over two days, okay? Three hours, one day for you, one day for the -- we lost 15 minutes. Yes, we lost 15 minutes in the beginning but to be honest with you, I have still got to -- some of the questions in the previous session, okay, were relevant and I couldn't stop Ms. Richardson but in reality he is being asked to confirm what others have testified about and which they have confirmed already.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the rest of the examination will be more pointed and we hope could conclude if not only as for a brief bit of tomorrow's time but there will be changes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 15 minutes here I would be able to concede but not more than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I do appreciate that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, I would ask you to go back to the document you were examining before the break and if you could -- unfortunately, we are running short on time so I would ask you to keep your comments as brief as possible. Just confirming or commenting briefly on the information contained. I would refer your attention to ERN number 02115070, at least the beginning portion on that page. On the English version, it is page 21. Now, if you look towards the middle portion on the B/C/S version, there is a reference to Hamdija, and just to be brief, there is mention by him that "the Court is not functioning and trouble makers" -- "we do not have a state or authorities to -- or authority so we have to do the best we can. Troublemakers should be detained for three days then put on trial." So also, right after that, there is a reference to the military police and the civilian police. And I would ask you if you could keep your comments brief, if you recall having -- being present when this discussion took place and if you look at the next page so that you can just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer that question first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand the first part of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The first part of the question is: Ms. Richardson has read out to you a part from the -- these minutes and she is asking you whether you recall this debate going on, taking place, at that meeting of the 9th of November of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have before me a version which is not typed out. It's handwritten and the copy is very bad. It's very difficult for me to read anything here. It's hard for me to find my way around this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I appreciate that. Let me read out to you the two -- the two parts myself and forget the text that you have there. The interpreters will try to help me out by interpreting to you. There is a part here which a certain Hamdija allegedly says the following: "There is still some shooting. When this is not done properly everything goes downhill. In these matters we should start from the commander." And then there is Becir who allegedly says the following: "We are all being honest. We are also to blame. Units are stealing from other units. If a vehicle belongs to the armed forces and if someone is a member of the armed forces, the civilian police do not have the right to intervene." And then there is a note which says "Conclusion, file a report against the unit commander and pass it off to the staff." And then there is the next bulleted entry which says, "The Court is not functioning. We do not have a state or authorities as we -- so we have to do the best we can. Troublemakers should be detained for three days and then put on trial." And then supposedly someone also says, "The military police and the civilian police include VES military occupational speciality in the JNA Yugoslav People's Army." Do you remember this kind of debate going on during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. This debate was conducted at the meeting concerning the chaos caused by the war and the fact that all organs had ceased functioning. The police, the court, the executive government, the legislative branch of government had all stopped functioning in 1992 so that individuals were committing acts which were not allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, your next question, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: There is also a mention, Mr. Omerovic, in the same document. It states that the court cannot pass final judgments, it has not been formed properly, it is a preventive task. Could you comments on whether or not that was said by anyone in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was -- this was said at the meeting. In Srebrenica, the court could be re-established but all the appeals courts were outside Srebrenica, either in Tuzla or in Sarajevo. So that if a court was organised and if it started working, we could not have judgement that was final, and there would be no point in having the court then. Whether it was Zulfo Tursunovic who said that or somebody else on the basis of the opinion I had previously presented to Mr. Masic, saying that final judgements could not be passed in the regular procedure. Because Srebrenica was surrounded, we could not deliver the appeals briefs to Tuzla or Sarajevo. We were unable to do that so that even had we organised a court and got it functioning, it could not have completed the job. We could only have done part of the job and then we would have had to stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: My final -- thank you. My final question with respect to this document, if you look further towards the end of the page, it's the beginning of 021157072, it states, it's on page 22 of the English and on the B/C/S it's 5072, it states, "a military court has been set up, legal officer Rasid [phoen], to work in the police. If Rasid doesn't turn up, Omerovic will work for the police." Could you comment on that, tell us -- tell Your Honours whether or not that was said during the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: I must clarify this. I think that this meeting which was organised was erroneously organised in formal and legal terms. If the War Presidency reached some decisions, this had to be done according to the proper procedure. They had to be on the agenda. The War Presidency had to have rules of procedure, and there had to be a method of voting, and passing decisions. It says here military court, but I can assert with full responsibility that no decision was reached at that meeting about the establishing of a court, nor was there a vote on this. So I am absolutely certain that this was a misinterpretation by the person taking the minutes. The gentleman or rather Zulfo Tursunovic at one point said we shall try people, and on the basis of that sentence of his, you cannot conclude that a decision was reached that a court be established. It's correct what it says here that it was said that a lawyer Resid Sinanovic, he was referred to here. Before the war he was for a time the chief of the public security station or the chief of police, because there were no lawyers in the police, and he was to be engaged and at that time he was in a village. I think it was, Podloznik where he had family, and if he could not be reached, that I was to become active and work in the police. This was an agreement, but in formal and legal terms, there was no vote. So it was not a formal decision. It was more like a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the last question that I have with respect to that document. Thank you to the usher for assisting. Mr. Omerovic, had you met Zulfo Tursunovic prior to your arrival in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I had never met him before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you have any knowledge of him, aside from the fact that you just stated that you hadn't met him personally, did you hear anything about him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, haven't we heard this from others? Do you need to waste your time with this witness on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm about to put an exhibit to the witness and I would like to lay the foundational questions. However, if I can put the picture, the photograph, right now to the witness in the interests of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, can you describe Zulfo Tursunovic, his physical appearance?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: I met him during the war. I didn't know him before. He is a very large man, tall, with bushy eyebrows. He looked like a man from the villages, like a man from the mountains.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, I'd like the usher's assistance in showing an exhibit to this witness, and we do have copies to distribute to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: This photograph is on sanction as well it's ERN number 03592919. Mr. Omerovic, please take a look at this photograph that is in front of you and tell the Trial Chamber whether you recognise this person and who this person is.

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is Mr. Zulfo Tursunovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to go to another area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to tender this?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I do, and if we could have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes what's the next number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P548. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: My next series of questions, Mr. Omerovic, has to do with your knowledge of the police. Could you first tell us if you were aware of the presence of the civilian police in Srebrenica during the period of time that you were -- that you were there?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: On my arrival in Srebrenica, I observed that in the police building where up to the outbreak of the war the public security station of Srebrenica had been located, I observed that the police were located there. According to my observation, there were very few policemen who had uniforms, only a few policemen had uniforms, so you couldn't see them around town because they weren't wearing uniforms, they didn't have vehicles, they didn't have any equipment, they didn't have all the things that a police force should have. I had the impression that as the police in early April 1992 had simply dissolved, that men --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you at this point. I'd like you to answer my question with respect to the time that you were in Srebrenica, not before. So if you could just tell us, because we are short on time, whether or not you were aware of the person who was the chief of police in Srebrenica during the time you were present.

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: At the first meeting I attended, which we have just talked about, the War Presidency, an extended meeting, then I noticed that Mr. Becir Bogilovic was the chief of police until he was evacuated and sent to Tuzla because he was wounded in the leg and he walked with a stick. So when he came to this meeting, he was walking with a stick. After he was evacuated for Tuzla, the police station was taken over by Mr. Hakija Meholjic and he was the chief of the public security station in Srebrenica until the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now with respect to the military police, could you tell Your Honours if you were aware of the presence of the military police in Srebrenica during the time you were present?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: As for the military police, I can say that I observed only the commander of the military police, although he didn't have any insignia either. The military police, how shall I put it, didn't have insignia. In this wartime situation they collected some men who carried out these police duties but you couldn't recognise them by uniforms or white belts or pistols. You couldn't tell that they were policemen. I only found out that the commander of the military policemen was around because this was a dangerous person who behaved like a local sheriff. Everybody in the town was afraid of him. He walked around with pistols and a rifle. He wore a hat, and I thought that he was a dangerous person and he, instead of introducing law and order, he was the one actually causing chaos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mirsad Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to mover to the next exhibit that I will be using, and that's P458.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While the exhibit is being located, Mr. Omerovic, please try to restrict your answers to the question -- I mean, don't try to feed us more information than you are being asked, and if a question can be answered in -- by a mere yes or no, then please answer yes or no, without giving any more details, such as these last two questions, were you aware of the presence of the military police and your answer should have been yes or no. And then if you need to explain something, you tell us, and we will allow you to explain.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Omerovic, if you could -- I'm sorry, if the usher could place the English version on the ELMO, we would appreciate that, and the hard copy of the B/C/S can be given to the witness. Now, Mr. Omerovic, if you could take a look at this document and could you just state for the record whether you saw this document prior to your arrival in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you turn to page 3 of the -- excuse me, page 3 of the English -- sorry, page 2 of the English, page 3 -- page 3 of the B/C/S, there is a date in the top right-hand corner so we are making sure you're following. It's the 3rd of December 1992, and it states "The following policemen attended the scheduled staff meeting at the military police station." What I would like to you do is look at the list of the individuals and tell us the Trial Chamber, if you recognise any of the individuals on this list and whether or not they were policemen, as far as you were -- as far as you were -- as far as you know, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: I recognise a few names here, under number 4, Safet Muhic, and then Huran [phoen] Hasanovic, then number 11 and number 13, Dzananovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, they were police officers in Srebrenica during the time you were present?

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: I know that Dzananovic and Huran Hasanovic were policemen in the civilian police from 1993. After the public security station was taken over by Mr. Hakija Meholjic. They were in the regular civilian police force. I'm not aware that they were in the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could turn to page -- it appears to be page 12 of the B/C/S and page 5 of the English, -- excuse me, it's actually page 11 of the B/C/S. There is a date in the corner, the 6th of December 1992, and it details a list of things missing from the house of Alija Zulic Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. [phoen] and just if you look at this it's clearly food items, if you would agree with that. And finally, towards the end, the very last sentence, it states "civilian police found them in Mirzada Hodzic's [phoen] house." My question with respect to this information is whether or not this reflects some of the incidents that occurred in Srebrenica during the time you were present.

utterances.speaker: MENSUD OMEROVIC
utterances.text: There were individual incidents of theft, just as there are during peacetime. Food was scarce and probably someone knew there was food in a certain house and stole it. I'm sure that there were cases like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. And if you would turn to the next page, I would like to you look at, which is page 10 of the English -- pardon me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While this is going on, previously, I remember when you first referred him to the previous extract, you said it's on page 5 and the English text -- in actual fact, it's on page 9, because page 5 refers to the 5th of November -- 5th of December, while the incident you mentioned occurs on page 9 in the English text.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Page 10 and it's page 12 of the English and -- excuse me, the B/C/S it's 03593135. It's dated the 7th of December and there is reference to the police. "It says send a patrol to Borak every day to check the guard and to bring in military age men who are avoiding guard duty." My question to you is: Were you were aware that these were some of the duties of the military police during the time you were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The witness didn't accept there was a military police so the question is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
